uncited: They are distinct from [CSG Difference](1238-csg-difference.md) in that they explicitly model the geometry of the intersection region (e.g., fillets or grooves) rather than simply subtracting volumes.
The core mathematical property distinguishing these operators from generic smooth minimums is their preservation of Lipschitz continuity.
Creates a chamfered edge between two objects.
Creates a pipe-like structure connecting two objects, effectively calculating the distance to a cylinder of radius $r$ centered at the intersection corner.
Engraves a feature into object $a$ using object $b$ as a tool, with radius $r$.
Creates a groove with specific radii $r_a$ and $r_b$ for the two sides.
Creates a series of columns or pillars at the intersection of two objects.

These operators were developed to address the limitations of standard boolean SDF operations, which produce sharp, non-smooth edges that can cause artifacts in ray marching if not handled with complex logic.
They are widely used in procedural geometry generation, voxel art, and real-time rendering where smooth, continuous distance fields are required for stable marching steps and normal estimation.

Source [S2] corroborates this, stating they preserve Lipschitz continuity 'better than standard smooth minimums when gradients are at right angles.' The claim accurately reflects the provided evidence.

Standard smooth minimums can violate the Lipschitz condition (where the gradient magnitude exceeds 1) when combining SDFs, leading to ray marching artifacts [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that standard smooth minimums can violate the Lipschitz condition (gradient magnitude > 1) when combining SDFs, leading to ray marching artifacts. Source [S1] explicitly notes that 'Unlike popular 'smooth minimum' operators... these do not lose Lipschitz continuity in many cases... If the gradients of the two SDFs are off by more than 30 degrees, the Lipschitz condition will no longer hold, causing artifacts.' This implies that the standard operators (which the new ones are contrasted against) do lose Lipschitz continuity under similar conditions, leading to the artifacts mentioned. Source [S2] corroborates this by stating 'Lipschitz continuity is lost if the gradients of the two SDFs are off by more than 30 degrees or if surfaces are parallel and close, causing artifacts.' Thus, the evidence supports the claim.
